subject: Chemistry
description: Reaction rate, factors affecting rate, catalysts, activation energy, order of reaction

questions.stem: The RATE of a chemical reaction generally INCREASES when:

options.option_text: The temperature of the reaction mixture is lowered
The concentration of the reactants is increased
The total volume of the container is enlarged
An inert gas is added at constant volume

questions.explanation: Higher concentration → more collisions per second → higher rate. Other rate-boosting factors: higher temperature (more high-energy collisions), larger surface area (for solids), suitable catalyst. Distractor 1 — lowering temperature SLOWS reactions (rule of thumb: rate halves per 10 °C drop). Distractor 3 — enlarging volume DILUTES reactants → slower. Distractor 4 — adding inert gas at constant volume doesn't change reactant concentrations.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: A CATALYST speeds up a reaction by:

options.option_text: Increasing the temperature of the reactant mixture
Providing a pathway with lower activation energy
Shifting the equilibrium toward the products side
Consuming itself rapidly during the chemical change

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Ea) — provides an alternative reaction path with a smaller energy barrier. More molecules now have enough energy → reaction proceeds faster. Catalyst is NOT consumed (regenerated by end of cycle). Catalysts do NOT shift equilibrium — they speed up forward + reverse equally; equilibrium position unchanged, only reached faster. Examples: enzymes (biological), Pt/Pd in catalytic converters, V₂O₅ in contact process, Ni in hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: ACTIVATION ENERGY is best understood as:

options.option_text: The total energy released by the reaction overall
The minimum energy reactants need to start reacting
The kinetic energy of every molecule in the system
The bond energy of the products formed in the reaction

questions.explanation: Activation energy (Ea) — the minimum energy barrier that reactant molecules must overcome to form products. Plotted as the 'hump' on a reaction-energy diagram. Lower Ea → faster reaction. Arrhenius equation k = A · exp(−Ea/RT) — a 10 °C rise often roughly doubles rate at moderate temperatures. Distractor 1 = enthalpy change ΔH (different concept — net energy released or absorbed). Distractor 3 = thermal kinetic energy (related but not Ea). Distractor 4 = bond dissociation energy (different).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: A reaction is said to be FIRST ORDER overall when:

options.option_text: The rate is independent of any reactant concentration
The rate is directly proportional to one reactant's concentration
The rate depends on the square of one reactant's concentration
The rate depends on the cube of any reactant's concentration

questions.explanation: First-order: rate = k[A]¹. Examples — radioactive decay (each atom decays independently), many enzymatic reactions at low substrate concentration. Half-life of first-order is concentration-INDEPENDENT (constant). Distractor 1 describes a ZERO order reaction (rate constant). Distractor 3 = SECOND order. Distractor 4 = THIRD order (rare).

questions.stem: A finely powdered solid reacts faster than the same mass in lump form because:

options.option_text: The solid's chemical composition becomes different
The surface area exposed to the other reactant increases
Powdered solids always contain higher-energy electrons
The reaction always occurs only at very high temperature

questions.explanation: Reaction rate depends on contact area between reactants. Powdering a solid increases its exposed surface area dramatically (a 1 cm cube has 6 cm² surface; chopping into 1 mm cubes gives 60 cm²). Faster collisions → faster reaction. Examples: powdered zinc reacts with HCl much faster than zinc strip; flour explosions in mills (huge surface). Distractor 1 — composition is unchanged. Distractor 3 — false; electrons don't change. Distractor 4 — false generalisation.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Enzymes are biological catalysts. Compared to inorganic catalysts, enzymes are typically:

options.option_text: Slower at the same temperature for the same reaction
Highly substrate-specific and active near body temperature
Always permanently consumed during the reaction cycle
Effective only above 100 °C, like steel-mill catalysts

questions.explanation: Enzymes are highly substrate-specific (lock-and-key / induced-fit model) and have an OPTIMUM temperature near body temperature (~37 °C in humans); above ~50-60 °C most denature and lose activity. They are FASTER per active site than inorganic catalysts (turnover number can be 10⁶-10⁹ /s for some enzymes). Examples: amylase (starch), pepsin (protein, acidic stomach), trypsin (protein, alkaline intestine). Distractor 1 — enzymes are typically much faster, not slower. Distractor 3 — like all catalysts, regenerated, not consumed. Distractor 4 — opposite of true; high temperatures denature enzymes.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: If the temperature of a reaction is raised by 10 °C, the rate typically:

options.option_text: Decreases to roughly half its original value
Roughly doubles, by a common rule of thumb
Stays exactly the same as it was before
Slows down because reactants now expand a lot

questions.explanation: A 10 °C rise typically doubles the rate of most chemical reactions at room temperature (rough rule of thumb; actual factor depends on activation energy via Arrhenius equation). Reason — more molecules cross the activation-energy barrier when temperature is higher, even though the increase in average kinetic energy per molecule is small. Distractor 1 — opposite (lowering 10°C halves the rate). Distractor 3 — wrong, temperature has a strong effect. Distractor 4 — false intuition.
